old:
The conclusion follows a process of elimination. Medications with an unpleasant taste are "generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form." M can't be a tablet, because its waxy ingredient can't take the heat. M can't be a soft-gel, because the company "does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology" and makes everything itself. Capsule is what's left.

But look at who the first rule covers: only medications with an unpleasant taste. Nothing tells us M tastes bad. If M tastes fine, the rule never applies, and M could come in a liquid, a powder, or anything else. The elimination only works if M is in the group the rule covers.

new:
The argument narrows the options. M cannot be a tablet, because its waxy ingredient cannot tolerate the heat. M cannot be a soft-gel, because the company lacks that technology and makes all its medications itself.

What would make capsule the likely choice? Medications with an unpleasant taste generally come in one of those three forms. But nothing tells us M has an unpleasant taste. Without that connection, the usual pattern gives us no reason to expect M to come in one of the three forms.

If M tastes unpleasant, the pattern applies to it. Two of the usual forms are ruled out, which supports capsule as the most likely remaining form. Notice the limit: "generally" allows exceptions. We are supporting "most likely," not proving that a capsule is the only possible outcome.
rationale: Preserve generally/most likely; remove deterministic arrow or guarantee language. Keep Strengthen label and credited B unchanged.
